keep: Check the motives of the sources before the sources — much of what you know arrived as propaganda.
lede: Buried under two thousand years of someone else's storytelling — mostly Roman propaganda and male fantasy.
copy: The real woman was the last pharaoh of Egypt. She was a Macedonian Greek who spoke perhaps nine languages, commanded a navy, and managed the wealthiest kingdom in the Mediterranean. She was reportedly the only Ptolemy in three centuries to bother learning Egyptian.

She allied with Caesar and then Antony — not as a seductress but as a head of state playing a desperate game against the rising power of Rome. She used marriage and alliance the way her male rivals used legions. For a time she nearly redirected the future of the ancient world. When Antony's cause collapsed at Actium, she chose suicide over being paraded through Rome in chains.

Her afterlife (in Plutarch, Shakespeare and Hollywood) reveals more about each era's anxieties about powerful women than about Cleopatra herself. That is precisely why recovering the historical queen matters.

bio.why: A Pulitzer-winning biographer reading against hostile ancient sources to reconstruct a shrewd, capable ruler. Witty, rigorous, and it gives Cleopatra back her intelligence and agency.

contested: Schiff is a literary biographer rather than a classicist, and specialists note that she reconstructs interior life the sources cannot support. For the scholarly version, Duane Roller's Cleopatra: A Biography (2010) is drier and more cautious about what is actually known.
